files.lesson.md: --- order: 12 unit: brackets node: AC9M8A01 n3 title: Changing the subject summary: "A formula gives one letter from the others. To get a different letter, undo the steps in reverse order, doing the same to both sides: y = 3x + 5 becomes x = (y − 5)/3. Check by substituting." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "A formula gives you one thing from the others. Sometimes you need it to work the other way round." connection: target-average # data/connections/maths.yml (pilot: opening situation and Make; documentation only) uses: [AC9M7ST01 n2] # the mean, for the opening question and Make app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8168 url: http://127.0.0.1:8168/index.html readySelector: "#sl-w" layout: full explainPicture: { ref: formula.yml#explain-pic, caption: "$P = 2l + 2w$ rearranged: $w = (P - 2l) \\div 2$. With $P = 20$ and $l = 6$: $w = (20 - 12) \\div 2 = 4$." } explainClip: query: { code: "@formula.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain } caption: "Turn the formula around" say: "Changing the subject turns a formula around." clip: - caption: { text: "P = 2l + 2w gives P from l and w.", say: "This formula gives P from l and w." } - wait: 400 - caption: { text: "Undo + 2l, then × 2: w = (P − 2l) ÷ 2.", say: "Undo the add, then the times: w is P take two l, halved." } - wait: 600 - caption: { text: "P = 20, l = 6: w = (20 − 12) ÷ 2 = 4. The board agrees.", say: "Twenty take twelve is eight, halved is four. The board agrees." } - click: Make w bigger - click: Make w bigger - expect: { selector: "#gpanel", contains: "= 20" } - wait: 1200 --- Your marks so far are 62, 70 and 74, and you'd like to finish on an average of 70. What do you need on the last test? Have a guess first. The average formula works out an average from your marks, but here you know the average you want and need one of the marks. So the formula has to be turned around. You'll practise that on a formula you already know, the perimeter of a rectangle, and then come back to your marks at the end. We'll assume every test counts the same and is out of 100. A formula like $P = 2l + 2w$ gives $P$ when you know $l$ and $w$. $P$ is the **subject**: the letter on its own on one side. Sometimes you know $P$ and want $w$. **Changing the subject** rearranges the formula so $w$ is on its own. You undo the steps, as when you solved equations, but with letters. ## Predict: how wide? ```step stage: predict insight: "Working out the width with numbers before seeing any formula shows whether they take off both lengths before halving; the formula comes later, as the record of what they did." check: type: predict q: "You've got 20 m of fencing to go all the way round a rectangular garden bed, and it has to be 6 m long. How wide can it be?" options: ["4 m", "7 m", "8 m", "14 m"] actual: "4 m. The two lengths use 6 + 6 = 12 m, which leaves 8 m for the two widths, so each width is 4 m. 7 m takes off only one length before halving; 8 m is both widths together; 14 m takes off one length and stops." smaller: check: { type: number, q: "Take off the two 6 m lengths first. How many metres of fence are left for the two widths?", answer: 8, explain: "6 + 6 = 12 m goes on the lengths, so 20 − 12 = 8 m is left for both widths together." } ``` Here's the fence laid out in one straight line: two lengths and two widths. ## Run: check with numbers ```step stage: run insight: "Finding w on the board for P = 20 and l = 6 settles the prediction, and shows that the formula as written makes you search for w." try: { playground: board, starter: "formula.yml#run", height: 520 } check: { type: board, text: "Set $l = 6$, then find the $w$ that makes $P = 20$. Was your prediction right?", when: "P = 20 and l = 6" } ``` The board works the formula forwards, so you have to hunt for $w$. Next you'll write down what you did with the numbers, and then you won't need to hunt. ## Investigate: undo in reverse order ```step stage: investigate insight: "The bar model records what students did with the fence, row by row, so the rearranged formula is that record in symbols; then the same move on other formulas. Jo's mistake divides only one term." tasks: - check: type: question q: "Which formula records what you did with the fence?" options: - "$w = (P - 2l) \\div 2$" - "$w = P - 2l \\div 2$" - "$w = P \\div 2 - 2l$" - "$w = (P + 2l) \\div 2$" answer: 0 feedback: [null, "That halves only the two lengths. In the picture you halved what was left.", "That halves the whole fence first, then takes off two whole lengths.", "That adds the lengths on, but you took them off."] explain: "Take off the two lengths (P − 2l), then halve what is left: w = (P − 2l) ÷ 2. The brackets keep 'what is left' together." - check: type: answer q: "Make $x$ the subject of $y = 2x + 7$." answer: "x = (y - 7)/2" form: subject x feedback: - ["x = y/2 - 7", "Halve the whole side: undo + 7 first, then halve."] - ["x = (y + 7)/2", "Undo + 7 by taking away 7."] - ["x = y - 7/2", "Halve all of y − 7, so (y − 7)/2."] explain: "y − 7 = 2x, then halve both sides: x = (y − 7)/2. Check: y = 17 gives x = 5, and 2 × 5 + 7 = 17." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#jo" text: "Jo makes $x$ the subject of $y = 4x - 3$. Click the line where her working goes wrong." answer: 2 fault: logic misconception: divide-one-term explain: "Line 2: dividing the right side by 4 divides both terms, so (4x − 3) ÷ 4 = x − 3/4, not x − 3. Undo − 3 first: y + 3 = 4x, so x = (y + 3)/4." - check: type: working q: "Make $x$ the subject of $y = 3x + 5$. Write one step per line." start: "y = 3x + 5" form: subject x example: ["y - 5 = 3x", "x = (y - 5)/3"] wrong: [["y/3 = x + 5", "x = y/3 - 5"], ["y - 5 = 3x"]] explain: "Undo + 5: y − 5 = 3x. Undo × 3: x = (y − 5)/3." ``` ### Write it down Here's what you did with the fence, one row at a time. Each row is a line of the formula. Which formula says the same thing? ### Undo the last step first $x$ was multiplied by 3, then 5 was added. Undo in reverse order: take away 5, then divide by 3. ```worked y = 3x + 5 :: $x$ was multiplied by 3, then 5 was added. y - 5 = 3x :: Undo the last step first: take 5 from both sides. \frac{y - 5}{3} = x :: Undo $\times 3$: divide the whole of both sides by 3. x = \frac{y - 5}{3} :: Write the subject on the left. y = 11: x = \frac{11 - 5}{3} = 2 :: Check by substituting: $3 \times 2 + 5 = 11$. ✓ ``` Try one: make $x$ the subject of $y = 2x + 7$. ### Find the mistake Read Jo's working one line at a time. Which step did she do first? ### Your working Write each step on its own line. The checker marks the first line that does not follow. ## Modify: one change at a time ```step stage: modify insight: "One change at a time: a context checked on the board, one step, a minus sign, undoing a divide, a fraction in the formula, then the edge case of a subject that is subtracted." try: { playground: board, starter: "formula.yml#vary", height: 520 } tasks: - starter: "formula.yml#vary" hint: ["w = (P − 2l) ÷ 2.", "(26 − 16) ÷ 2."] check: { type: board, text: "Use $w = (P - 2l) \\div 2$ to find $w$ when $P = 26$ and $l = 8$. Set the board to check.", when: "P = 26 and l = 8", explain: "(26 − 16) ÷ 2 = 5, and 2 × 8 + 2 × 5 = 26." } - check: type: answer q: "One step: make $x$ the subject of $y = x + 9$." answer: "x = y - 9" form: subject x feedback: - ["x = y + 9", "Undo + 9 by taking away 9."] explain: "Take 9 from both sides: x = y − 9." - check: type: answer q: "A minus sign: make $x$ the subject of $y = 5x - 4$." answer: "x = (y + 4)/5" form: subject x feedback: - ["x = (y - 4)/5", "Undo − 4 by adding 4."] - ["x = y/5 + 4", "Undo − 4 first, then divide the whole side by 5."] explain: "Add 4: y + 4 = 5x. Divide by 5: x = (y + 4)/5." - check: type: answer q: "Undo a divide: make $d$ the subject of $v = \\dfrac{d}{t}$ (speed = distance ÷ time)." answer: "d = vt" form: subject d feedback: - ["d = v/t", "d was divided by t. Undo it by multiplying by t."] explain: "Multiply both sides by t: d = vt. Check: 60 km/h for 2 h is 120 km." - check: type: answer q: "A fraction: make $h$ the subject of $A = \\dfrac{bh}{2}$ (area of a triangle)." answer: "h = 2A/b" form: subject h feedback: - ["h = A/(2b)", "Undo ÷ 2 by multiplying by 2: 2A = bh."] - ["h = 2A - b", "h is multiplied by b, so divide by b."] explain: "Multiply by 2: 2A = bh. Divide by b: h = 2A/b." - check: type: answer q: "Edge case: make $x$ the subject of $y = 7 - x$." answer: "x = 7 - y" form: subject x feedback: - ["x = y - 7", "Check with numbers: x = 2 gives y = 5, and 5 − 7 is not 2."] explain: "Add x to both sides: y + x = 7. Take y away: x = 7 − y. Check: x = 2, y = 5, and 7 − 5 = 2." ``` ### Check on the board Each task changes one thing. ### One step No board from here: undo the steps, then check with numbers. ### A minus sign ### Undo a divide ### A fraction ### The subject is subtracted ## Practise: rearrange and check ```step stage: practise insight: "Rearranging real formulas with full working, mixed; dividing only one term is the planted slip, and the review keeps factorising fresh." tasks: - check: type: answer q: "A plumber charges $c = 50h + 80$ dollars for $h$ hours. Make $h$ the subject." answer: "h = (c - 80)/50" form: subject h feedback: - ["h = c/50 - 80", "Undo + 80 first, then divide the whole side by 50."] - ["h = (c + 80)/50", "Undo + 80 by taking away 80."] explain: "c − 80 = 50h, so h = (c − 80)/50. Check: h = 2 gives c = 180, and (180 − 80)/50 = 2." - check: type: working q: "Make $w$ the subject of $P = 2l + 2w$. Write one step per line." start: "P = 2l + 2w" form: subject w example: ["P - 2l = 2w", "w = (P - 2l)/2"] wrong: [["P - 2l = 2w", "w = P - 2l/2"], ["P/2 = l + 2w"]] explain: "Undo + 2l: P − 2l = 2w. Halve both sides: w = (P − 2l)/2." - check: type: answer q: "Use your formula: what is $w$ when $P = 30$ and $l = 9$?" answer: "6" feedback: - ["21", "Take 2l, not l: 30 − 18 = 12, then halve."] - ["12", "Halve as well: 12 ÷ 2."] explain: "(30 − 18) ÷ 2 = 6. Check: 2 × 9 + 2 × 6 = 30." - check: type: answer q: "Review: factorise $6x - 15$ fully." answer: "3(2x - 5)" form: factorised feedback: - ["3(2x + 5)", "The minus comes too: −15 ÷ 3 = −5."] explain: "HCF 3: 3(2x − 5)." ``` ### A formula in context ### Full working ### Use it ### Review: factorising ## Make: back to your marks ```step stage: make insight: "Coming back to the opening question: rearranging the average formula for the last mark (undo ÷ n, then + S), then using it, puts the lesson's move to work on a question students ask for themselves." tasks: - hint: ["x had S added, then the total was divided by n. Undo the last step first.", "Multiply both sides by n: nA = S + x. Then take S from both sides."] check: type: answer q: "With $n$ tests, the average is $A = \\dfrac{S + x}{n}$, where $S$ is the total of your marks so far and $x$ is the last mark. Make $x$ the subject." answer: "x = n*A - S" form: subject x feedback: - ["x = A/n - S", "Undo ÷ n by multiplying both sides by n."] - ["x = n*(A - S)", "Undo the last step first: × n before − S."] - ["x = n*A + S", "Undo + S by taking S away."] explain: "Multiply both sides by n: nA = S + x. Take S from both sides: x = nA − S." - hint: ["S is the total of the three marks so far; n = 4 and A = 70.", "S = 206, so x = 4 × 70 − 206."] check: type: number q: "Your marks so far are 62, 70 and 74. Use your formula: what do you need on the fourth test to average 70?" answer: 74 feedback: - [70, "That is the average you want. Use your formula for the mark you need."] - [280, "That is the total you need, nA. Take away what you already have."] - [206, "That is the total so far, S."] explain: "S = 206, n = 4, A = 70: x = 4 × 70 − 206 = 280 − 206 = 74. Check: (206 + 74) ÷ 4 = 70." ``` ### Turn it around Here are your marks as a bar model. The top bar is the total you need; the bottom bar is what you've got, plus the last test. Work it out on paper first, one step per line, the way the bar model goes. Then type your formula and check it with numbers: if your marks were 60 and 80, the average is 70. ### Your last test Check your answer by putting it back into the average. Stretch: if the last test is out of 100, what is the highest average you could still get? ## Make: a target pace, on paper ```step stage: make insight: "Time = pace × distance gives the time from the pace; a target time asks the other way round. Rearranging first, then putting the numbers in, is the step inside a question people really ask." hint: ["p was multiplied by d. What undoes multiplying?", "Divide both sides by d, then put the numbers in."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "You want to run 8 km in 44 minutes (made up for the task). Time = pace × distance, so $t = pd$, where the pace $p$ is in minutes per kilometre. What pace do you need?" steps: - ["$t = pd$, with $t = 44$ and $d = 8$", "write the formula and what you know"] - ["$p$ was multiplied by $d$, so divide both sides by $d$: $p = \\dfrac{t}{d}$", "undo the multiplying, on both sides"] - ["$p = 44 \\div 8 = 5.5$ minutes per kilometre", "put the numbers in last"] - ["Check: $5.5 \\times 8 = 44$", "put the pace back into the original formula"] picks: - step: 2 q: "How do you get $p$ on its own from $t = pd$?" options: - "Divide both sides by $d$" - "Subtract $d$ from both sides" - "Multiply both sides by $d$" answer: 0 feedback: [null, "$p$ is multiplied by $d$, not added to it. Subtracting does not undo that.", "That multiplies by $d$ a second time. Undo multiplying by dividing."] answer: "5.5" tolerance: 0.001 answerLabel: "Pace (minutes per km)" feedback: - ["352", "That multiplies 44 by 8. $p$ was multiplied by $d$, so divide by $d$."] - ["36", "That takes 8 from 44. Undo multiplying by dividing."] criteria: - "I made $p$ the subject before I put any numbers in." - "I divided both sides by $d$." - "I checked that 5.5 × 8 gives 44." explain: "$p = t \\div d = 44 \\div 8 = 5.5$ minutes per kilometre, which is 5 minutes 30 seconds. Check: $5.5 \\times 8 = 44$." ``` Do this one in your book, not on the screen. The distance and time are made up for the task, and a real run has hills and a tired finish. Write the formula, rearrange it for the pace, put the numbers in, check, and type the pace. **Also used in** - **Running pace.** Time = pace × distance. Turn it around to find the pace you need for a target time. - **A US weather forecast.** The conversion formula gives °F from °C. Turned around, it gives °C from °F. - **Science.** Speed = distance ÷ time, turned around for how long a trip takes. ```teacher summary: Students rearrange formulas to change the subject by undoing the steps in reverse order on both sides, and check each rearrangement by substituting numbers, on a formula board that works the original forwards (AC9M8A01, node 3). time: 45 timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 15 min · Modify 12 min · Practise and Make 10 min struggle: Undoing the steps in reverse order. Ask students to say what was done to the letter first and last, before they write anything. goals: - I can make a given letter the subject of a formula by undoing the steps in reverse order. - I can do the same to the whole of both sides, so I divide every term. - I can check a rearranged formula by substituting numbers. before: > Do the Run board and the working check yourself first. Students need solving equations by backtracking and the balance method (Year 7 equations unit), substituting into formulas, and the two lessons before (expanding and factorising). Pilot (Oct 2026): the lesson opens with a real question (what do I need on the last test to average 70?) and Make comes back to it; "Also used in" closes it. Rearranging is a skill people rarely do by hand outside study, so this is an "enabler" use: the step inside a task students do ask about. The middle of the lesson still uses the perimeter formula. Tell us whether the switch between the two contexts gets in the way. The one idea: changing the subject is solving an equation with letters. Undo what was done to the letter, last step first, doing the same to both sides. The common mistake is dividing only one term (y = 4x − 3 becomes y ÷ 4 = x − 3); it is planted after the method, in Jo's working. Undoing the − 3 first avoids it. Answers are marked by form and value: the subject must be on its own on the left, and the formula must agree with the original for every value. An equal formula in another shape, such as x = y/2 − 7/2 for (y − 7)/2, is marked right. running: - "Predict: take a show of hands on the width; ask someone who said 4 m what they did first. That order (take off the lengths, then halve) is the formula they will write in Investigate." - "Run: ask students to say why the board needed trial and error and the rearranged formula did not." - "Investigate: model the worked example live as a flow: x → × 3 → + 5 → y, then backwards: y → − 5 → ÷ 3 → x." - "Modify: before the edge case y = 7 − x, ask: what is x if y = 5? Most find 2 mentally; then ask how they did it." - "Make: back to the opening marks. Ask for guesses first (many say 70, or 78 to make up for the 62); then ask students to show the formula they wrote and how they checked it." - "Paper: Make's rearrangement is done on paper first, one step per line; the page checks only the final formula. Books out, and look for the order of the undoing." - "Pace: the target-pace task is worked in books; the page marks the pace (5.5) and the reason for dividing by d. Books out, and look for the rearranged formula before any number goes in." stuck: - see: A student divides only one term (Jo's mistake). ask: Put in x = 2. Does your formula give back the y you started with? fix: Undo the add or subtract first, so there is only one term left to divide. - see: A student undoes the steps in the wrong order (x = y/3 − 5 from y = 3x + 5). ask: What was done to x first? What was done last? fix: "Draw the flow: x → × 3 → + 5 → y. Go back along it from y." - see: A student gets lost with letters. ask: What would you do if the formula were 11 = 3x + 5? fix: Solve it with the number, then do exactly the same steps with y. stretch: Make l the subject of P = 2l + 2w, then r the subject of C = 2πr, then x the subject of ax + b = c. support: Give a number version first (11 = 3x + 5), then the letter version beside it, step for step. leads: > This completes AC9M8A01: expanding, factorising and changing the subject. Where it leads: formulas in science (v = d/t, F = ma, ρ = m/V), linear relations (y = mx + c rearranged for x), and in Years 9 and 10 rearranging formulas with the subject in more than one term (factorise it out). exit: q: Make x the subject of y = 6x − 2, then check it with x = 3. a: "x = (y + 2)/6. Check: x = 3 gives y = 16, and (16 + 2)/6 = 3." explain: > To **change the subject**, undo what was done to the letter you want, **last step first**, doing the same to the whole of both sides. $y = 3x + 5$: $x$ was multiplied by 3, then 5 was added. Take 5 away: $y - 5 = 3x$. Divide by 3: $x = \dfrac{y - 5}{3}$. Check by putting in numbers: $x = 2$ gives $y = 11$, and $\dfrac{11 - 5}{3} = 2$. ```

files.working.txt:
# Jo's working for the "find the mistake" task. Plain text: students click the wrong line, nothing runs.

# region: jo
Make x the subject of y = 4x − 3.
Divide both sides by 4: y ÷ 4 = x − 3.
Add 3 to both sides: y ÷ 4 + 3 = x.
So x = y/4 + 3.
# endregion
